title: Mar. 1,  2026 | The 2nd Sunday in Lent
author: The Rev'd Charles Everson
description: This morning's sermon is a little different than those I normally preach. I want to invite you to sit with me inside the mind of Nicodemus, one of the characters in this morning's Gospel, and explore ...
content:
This morning's sermon is a little different than those I normally preach. I want to invite you to sit with me inside the mind of Nicodemus, one of the characters in this morning's Gospel, and explore how he might have experienced this encounter with Jesus.

My name is Nicodemus. I am a Pharisee and a member of the Sanhedrin, the council that governs the religious life of our people. I have spent my entire adult life studying the Torah, observing the commandments, and teaching others to do the same. I know the law and the prophets. I know the tradition of the elders. If you had asked anyone in Jerusalem to name a man who understood the things of God, my name would have been at the top of the list.

I came to him at night, and I'm not ashamed of that. I've heard preachers over the years use my nocturnal visit as evidence of cowardice, as though I crept through the dark streets of Jerusalem because I was too scared to be seen in the daylight. The truth is, I came at night because the night was the only time I could think clearly. During the day, I was always Nicodemus the Pharisee, Nicodemus the teacher, Nicodemus the member of the council. At night, I was just someone with questions.

Years later, I came to see that the darkness I walked through that night was not only in the streets but in my own heart. And I had questions. I had watched him. I had seen the signs he performed—not tricks nor theater, but miracles that didn't make any sense to me or to others, that pressed against the categories I had spent a lifetime constructing. I could not explain him, and I am someone who has built his entire life on the ability to explain things.

So I went to him at night, and I said what I genuinely believed. "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher who has come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do apart from the presence of God." I thought that was a perfectly reasonable opening. I was paying him a compliment. I was being collegial, even generous. He didn't even respond to it. Instead, he looked at me with those eyes—the eyes of a man who sees directly through whatever you are saying to him. And he said, "Very truly I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God without being born from above."

I had no idea what he meant, and I told him so. I asked the obvious question about re-entering the mother's womb, which I know sounds ridiculous, but I was a literal man trained in a very literal tradition, and I was doing my best. Then he said it again differently: "No one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and the Spirit." I didn't know then what he meant, but I know now. He was not speaking of a change of mind or a reformed life. He was speaking of a new creation—something done to you, not by you. A death and a rebirth in water, the Spirit hovering over the deep as it was at creation.

What he was describing was not self-improvement; it was something closer to drowning and being pulled out alive. What I did not say, but what I felt at that moment was this: I'm too old for this. Not in terms of years, though I was not young, but in that my categories were already set. I had spent decades building the architecture of my worldview, and what he was describing—this birth from above, the wind that blows where it will—sounded like an invitation to demolish everything I had constructed and start again from nothing. "How can these things be?" I asked him. It was the most honest question I had ever asked.

He then proceeded to tell me how it was that I was a teacher of Israel and didn't understand these things. The answer, though I could not have articulated it then, is that I understood everything I had been taught and almost nothing that could not be taught. I knew the tradition, but I did not know the wind. And what terrified me was not that I couldn't understand it, but that I couldn't control it.

He told me that just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up. I didn't understand what he meant—not then—but after I watched them nail him to that tree, I understood. The very thing I could not look at became the thing that saved me. And then he said this: "For God so loved the world, not the righteous, not the learned, not the observant, but the world—this whole crazy world—that he gave his only Son, not to condemn it but to save it."

I kept returning to that, even after everything that happened—after the trial, after the cross, after the morning they found the tomb empty. I kept returning to that. I think that is still the question. I think it is the question sitting in this room right now, in every person who has come this morning with good intentions and genuine faith and carefully constructed categories of your own. "How can these things be?" I don't know, but I've come to believe that not knowing is not the end of the conversation. It is, in fact, where the conversation begins.

St. John mentions Nicodemus twice more in his Gospel. In chapter seven, Nicodemus speaks up quietly before the council in defense of the man they are trying to condemn. In chapter 19, after the crucifixion, he comes again in some sense out of the darkness, bringing a lavish quantity of spices to anoint the body. Nicodemus never delivers a speech of conversion. He never makes a public declaration of faith. He simply keeps showing up, doing the next faithful thing, the wind slowly working in him what he could never have worked in himself.

Dear friends, the season of Lent is for Nicodemuses. It is for people who come to God in the night, who still have more questions than answers, and who are learning slowly to let the wind blow where it will. In today's collect, we ask God to bring us again with penitent hearts and steadfast faith to embrace and hold fast the unchangeable truth of God's word, Jesus Christ. To embrace and hold fast not an argument, not a system of belief, but a person—the same person who sat with Nicodemus in the dark and did not send him away. Lent is long, and the night is real, but the one who sat with Nicodemus in the dark is...

title: May 24, 2026 | The Day of Pentecost
author: The Rev'd Charles Everson
description: There is a line in that sequence hymn this morning that has been rolling around in my mind and heart all week. The hymn is a translation of the medieval Latin 'Veni Sancte Spiritus,' the golden sequen...
content:
There is a line in that sequence hymn this morning that has been rolling around in my mind and heart all week. The hymn is a translation of the medieval Latin "Veni Sancte Spiritus," the golden sequence, likely by Archbishop of Canterbury Stephen Langton around the year 1200, and sung by the Western Church on this feast ever since. In the fourth stanza, the hymn names a series of things the Holy Spirit comes to do. The Spirit comes with soft rains to break our drought. The Spirit comes with rushing wind to shake our will. The Spirit comes with fire to melt our icy chill. And then this strange line: the Spirit comes to bring to light our perjuries.

It's an awfully strange thing to ask for. We don't normally come to church hoping to have our lives exposed. We come hoping to be comforted, strengthened, and drawn into the mystery of God here in the beauty of holiness. And yet the church, in her wisdom, has placed this petition at the heart of this hymn and asked us to sing it. The gospel we just heard tells us why. St. John's account of Pentecost is quieter than Luke's. There is no rushing wind, no tongues of fire, no multilingual praise. Instead, the frightened disciples are in a locked room. The risen Lord appears among them and shows them his wounds. And then he says, "Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I send you."

Then he breathes on them. The Greek verb John uses here is rare; it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It is the same verb the Greek Old Testament uses when God breathes the breath of life into Adam at the creation of the world. The risen Christ breathes on his disciples and says, "Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them. If you retain the sins of any, they are retained." The Holy Spirit is breathed for the forgiveness of sins. This is the very first thing the risen Lord says about why he's giving us the Spirit: for the forgiveness of sins.

And as it turns out, there cannot be forgiveness without truth-telling. You cannot be forgiven for what you will not name. You cannot be absolved of what you refuse to admit. And so the Spirit, who comes to forgive sins, must first bring our perjuries to light. That is what the author of this hymn understood. The Spirit's work of forgiveness begins with honesty. The word "perjury" is a strong word. It means more than a casual untruth; a perjury is a lie told under oath, a falsehood sworn as if it were the truth. The word is not in the original Latin text of the hymn; it is the choice of the translator. The Latin original says something starker still: without the Spirit's power, nothing in us is innocent.

The translator heard in that line all the lies we have sworn to and gave them a more poignant name: perjuries. And I think he was right. The most dangerous lies are not the ones we tell other people; they are the ones we tell ourselves over and over until we have built our lives on top of them and forgotten they were ever there. This is the work the Holy Spirit comes to do: to bring to light the things we have hidden from ourselves, the things we promised ourselves we would deal with someday but have quietly forgotten. The grudge we say we have let go but still dwell on in the wee hours of the night. The pattern of behavior we tell ourselves is harmless but have always known that it is not. The relationship we keep saying is fine but we really need to deal with. The addiction we keep saying is under control. The resentment we hold toward another person that we keep saying to ourselves is justified.

The Holy Spirit shines on all of it—gently, persistently, mercifully. The Spirit brings our perjuries to light. And this work of the Spirit isn't just about each of us as individuals. The Spirit who exposes our private self-deceptions is the same Spirit who exposes the falsehood at the heart of empire. The same Spirit who descended on the Apostles on Pentecost Day sent them out into the world to tell the truth in a world that did not want to hear it. They went out and told the truth about Rome: that Caesar is not Lord. They told the truth about the temple authorities: that the man they handed over to die was truly the Messiah, the Son of God. And they told the truth about the social order: that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.

Saint Peter, who had perjured himself three times in the courtyard of the high priest, became the apostle who would not stop telling the truth. Dear friends, you and I need the same Holy Spirit now in our world today. We need the Spirit who brings perjuries to light—not only our private lies, but the public ones, the shared ones, the polite falsehoods by which a society agrees to live while some of its members are crushed. We need the Spirit to keep us honest.

And so we come to this Mass this morning as those who need the Spirit's exposing light. Each of us has lies we have sworn to. Each of us has falsehoods we have built our lives on. Each of us is loved by a God whose mercy is more powerful than our self-deception. In a moment, as we do at nearly every Mass, we will confess our sins together. We will say, using words that most of us know by heart, that we have sinned against God in thought, word, and deed, by what we have done and by what we have left undone.

And then I will pronounce the words of absolution: "Almighty God, have mercy on you. Forgive you all your sins through our Lord Jesus Christ. Strengthen you in all goodness, and by the power of the Holy Spirit, keep you in eternal life." Of course, our Protestant cousins are right that you can go directly to God with your confession and be forgiven. You can confess in the silence of your own heart and be forgiven, but the absolution pronounced by a priest or a bishop is a different thing altogether. It is the Church doing what the risen Lord empowered her to do when he breathed his Spirit on the disciples and said, "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven."

I will proclaim to you the words of absolution with the Church's authority by the power of the Holy Spirit. We began with a strange prayer that the Spirit would bring our perjuries to light. It is not a prayer for the faint of heart, but it is the prayer of a people who trust that the God who exposes our lives does so in order to forgive us. And so let the light come. Let it fall on whatever you have hidden. And when you hear the words of absolution in a moment, do not ignore them as rote ritual that you have heard.

title: Apr. 19, 2026 | Easter 3
description: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Imagine two people walking away from the worst week of their lives. They aren't running, as running would require a destination. They...
content:
In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Imagine two people walking away from the worst week of their lives. They aren't running, as running would require a destination. They are simply moving, the way that grief makes you move—putting one foot in front of the other because standing still is somehow worse. The road to Emmaus stretches seven miles from Jerusalem, and every step takes them further from the place where it all fell apart. They are sad, confused, and full of despair.

As they are talking and discussing the fateful events they had witnessed, Jesus shows up. But for some reason, their eyes are kept from recognizing him. He asks them what they're talking about, and they respond by telling him about their shattered expectations. Jesus then begins to teach the two travelers and explain to them how the events they had experienced were the fulfillment of the scriptures of old. They still aren't convinced, but when Jesus tries to leave and head another direction, the two disciples urge him strongly to stay with them. Even though they still don't recognize him, his preaching and teaching from the scriptures apparently had enough impact on them that they want to spend more time with him.

When they sit down at the table, he breaks bread, blesses it, and gives it to them. And suddenly their eyes are opened. They realize that the man standing before them is the one in whom they had placed all their hope. The women who experienced the vision with the angel weren't insane after all. He has risen indeed. Jesus finally makes himself known to them in the breaking of the bread.

Now don't mishear me. As a priest, my duties include preaching and teaching the scriptures, as I'm doing now, and that certainly has its place. But preaching and teaching only reach so far into the depths of our being. From the age of 11 to 24, I was Southern Baptist and was taught that the normal way to commune intimately with God is by having what is called a quiet time—time by yourself in a room with the Bible, praying and studying the scriptures. Of course, corporate worship was important, and listening to sermons far lengthier than the one you are enduring now. But for me, anyway, there was something missing that I couldn't quite put my finger on until the day that I walked into a 13th-century church in Paris called Saint-Etienne-du-Mont, Saint Stephen of the Mount.

I was living in Paris and serving as a Baptist missionary, and I sang in a university choir. My first concert with them was in that very church, the one served for many years by the composer Maurice Duruflé and his wife, Marie Madeleine, as organists. During that concert, it dawned on me in an intensely emotional way that we were singing a choral mass setting in a building where the mass had been celebrated every day for nearly 500 years. I had seen the mass times on the way in and decided to attend their simple daily mass the next morning at 8:30 a.m. It was at that service that I first recognized the Lord in the breaking of the bread.

When the priest elevated the consecrated host for all to behold and said, "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world," my eyes were opened, and I knew what it was that I had been missing. Part of what hit me that day is that salvation is not merely a spiritual redemption of our hearts; it is also a physical redemption of our bodies. God's grace is more than a feeling. And thank God, because sometimes I wondered whether the funny feeling right here is the voice of God or indigestion. God sent Jesus to redeem our whole selves—heart, soul, mind, and body. He doesn't only share his love and grace with us by intangible means, like quiet prayer and the study of scripture, but perhaps even more importantly, by the gritty, tangible elements of water, bread, and wine.

God didn't send his Son to redeem us as a disembodied spirit, but as a human being with flesh and blood and bones. He doesn't leave us wondering whether the voice we are hearing is the voice of God or a ghost. He has given us the sacraments of the church, especially baptism and Holy Communion, as a sure and certain means by which we receive his inward and spiritual grace. As soon as their eyes were opened, the two disciples got up that same hour and went to find their friends, joyfully telling them that the Lord has risen indeed and that he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.

This sharing of the faith, sometimes called evangelism, conjures up images of street preachers with megaphones and door-to-door missionaries in foreign countries. But evangelism at its best is the natural sharing of the faith with those you already know and have a relationship with. While it should be intentional, evangelism should never be judgy or pushy or disrespectful. When we encounter God in our lives—whether it's through prayer, through the embrace of a friend, through the scriptures, or through the consecrated bread and wine of communion—it is natural to want to share the joy of that encounter with others, both in word and deed.

Here at Atonement, we celebrate the Eucharist every day, and the Eucharist is not the possession of a few, but the inheritance of all the baptized. Week after week, day after day, Jesus makes himself known to us in the breaking of the bread. I celebrate the Mass usually four or five times a week, and it is quite common for me to elevate the consecrated host and be taken back to that morning in Paris when I was 23 years old, when I first recognized Jesus in the breaking of the bread.

No matter how isolated or lonely or full of despair you may feel, no matter how your hopes and expectations may have been crushed, like the two travelers on the road to Emmaus, you are invited to recognize Jesus here at this altar. We break bread together not in isolation but in community with one another. God meets you where you are, no matter where you are in your journey, no matter your station in life. As we break bread together in a moment, let us ask the Lord to open the eyes of our faith. You may have heard the scriptures preached and taught throughout your life and yet find that something is still missing. You may recognize Jesus today in the breaking of the bread as you have for decades. Wherever you find yourself today, he is here, and he is making himself known to us in the breaking of the bread.

title: July 19, 2026 | Pentecost 8
author: The Rev'd Charles Everson
description: Last week, we heard the parable of the sower, and this week we hear the parable of the weeds, or the tares, as it is traditionally known. Despite having attended a rural Texas high school whose bigges...
content:
Last week, we heard the parable of the sower, and this week we hear the parable of the weeds, or the tares, as it is traditionally known. Despite having attended a rural Texas high school whose biggest student club was the Future Farmers of America, I am a city boy at heart and don't know the first thing about farming. Thankfully, others have written about some of the farming issues involved in this parable.

It begins with Jesus saying that the kingdom of heaven may be compared to someone who sowed good seed in his field. But while everyone was asleep, an enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and then went away. The weeds here are thought to be a specific plant called bearded Darnell. This plant looks identical to wheat above ground, but below, it wraps itself around the wheat, intertwining itself into the root system and taking away nutrients and moisture from the wheat. It is a deceptive little plant. Rather than producing seeds that are nutritious like wheat, Darnell seeds are toxic to humans and can cause anything from hallucination to death.

In Jesus' time, sowing Darnell in a field for the purposes of revenge was illegal, meaning it must have happened often enough to warrant such a law. In this parable, Jesus uses this noxious weed to illustrate evil. An enemy intentionally sowed these weeds among the wheat. When the farmhands discovered this, they proposed to the farmer that they go and gather the weeds. Well, like me, these farmhands were not up to speed on their horticulture. If they had been, they would have known that doing so would result in the wheat coming out of the ground at the same time, destroying the crop.

All too often, you and I become preoccupied with who is in and who is out. Like the farmhands, we think that we have what it takes—spiritually, mentally, emotionally—to separate the wheat from the weeds. But as in the parable, trying to separate the wheat from the Darnell actually hurts both plants. This phenomenon happens in the Church today when we try to separate the real Christians from those who have a different stance than we do on any particular issue. In trying to weed out those who are impure, we do damage to the faithful as well.

In the Church, our world is full of dichotomies, and it seems increasingly so, perhaps especially in politics. What is the solution to this tendency to divide the world in two? The farmer instructs the farmhands to let both the wheat and the weeds grow together until the harvest, when all will be revealed. For at the harvest, the wheat and Darnell bloom differently, and it becomes obvious which is which. Even then, it won't be up to us to decide who is in and who is out. Jesus tells us in the second part of the reading that the Son of Man will send his angels to do this work. Then and now, it is our job to trust that God will sort through the wheat and the weeds in a way that only God can do.

No matter how similar they look, no matter how intertwined the root systems are, God will send his angels, with the appropriate knowledge and skill, to separate the weeds out without damaging the wheat. While this parable is explicitly about the kingdom of heaven and thus the last things, I can't help but think that my own life is often like the farmer's infested field, with weeds and wheat intertwined in my heart, soul, and mind. Paul said it this way in the book of Romans: "For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate."

When someone begins to come to private confession regularly for the first time in their lives, it usually only takes two or three confessions before he or she says to me something like this: "Father, I keep confessing the same sins over and over. Is that normal?" Yes, yes it is. All of us are plagued with the temptation to commit specific sins over the course of our lives, each of us influenced by both nature and nurture. And no matter how holy we become, it is unlikely that our respective pet sins will change over time.

Usually, the next question is, "Well, since I keep confessing the same sins over and over, why do I do this at all?" Not to force an analogy into this parable, but perhaps the grace the penitent receives from God through absolution is like the water and nutrients the plants in the field receive for their sustenance. When we repent from our sins and intend to amend our lives, we only do so by God's grace. While we can't stop sinning completely on this side of the veil, we certainly can learn to trust God more and more in the midst of the sin and chaos of our hearts and of the world, holding fast to the hope that at the last day, God will send the reaper to bring in the harvest.

Last week, we heard St. John Chrysostom say that the sower keeps sowing on rocky ground because with human souls, the ground can change. Preaching on today's parable, he goes one step further—frankly further than botany allows. The master spares the weeds, St. Chrysostom says, because it is possible for the weeds themselves to become wheat. We know that bearded Darnell simply cannot become wheat. But grace does what plants cannot do, and the long delay before the harvest is not negligence on God's part; it is the space God has carved out for conversion—yours and mine, and even the person you were most tempted to yank up by the roots this week.

Every season the field grows unweeded is a season grace is still at work beneath the surface, down among the roots too tangled for anyone but God to figure out. That is why the Master waits. One more season, one more confession, one more time to receive Holy Communion. And so we wait too, drinking in the grace of God's Word and sacraments, growing toward a harvest we know will come but cannot yet see.

In a few moments, with wheat and weeds still intertwined in our hearts, we will present ourselves humbly before God at this altar rail, and God will feed us generously without first sorting us out. In the reading we heard from Romans, Paul promises that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory about to be revealed. At the harvest, what has been hidden all season will finally be seen—not the weeds, but the wheat that God, through His extravagant grace, has been making of us all along. Amen.

title: June 21, 2026 | The 4th Sunday after Pentecost
description: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. This passage from the Gospel of Matthew is a great passage for Christian militants, or so it seems at first. 'Go out into the light, ...
content:
In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. This passage from the Gospel of Matthew is a great passage for Christian militants, or so it seems at first. "Go out into the light, shout from the rooftops. Christ came not to bring peace, but a sword. Cling not to your fathers and mothers, but to Jesus. Cling not to this life, but give up your life for the sake of Christ." There is no middle-of-the-road, conciliatory Christianity here. No compromise, no accommodation, no middle path. Beyond a call to be a Christian militant, the reading goes, Jesus invites his disciples to share in his fate. This requires not only the loss of family and being outcast socially, but active hostility to the point of death.

In this way of reading it, Jesus encourages his disciples to live beyond fear. They know that God cares for them more than they can possibly care for anything themselves. They likewise know that their confession of Jesus wins them his recognition on the last day. These words have brought peace to many Christians over the centuries, but they can also bring fear and trepidation. This passage is a useful passage for those militant Christians who somehow enjoy confronting both fear and power. I don't know about you, but I wouldn't describe myself as a Christian militant. I no longer feel comfortable singing that old hymn, "Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus, Ye Soldiers of the Cross." I left that construct when I chose to leave my Southern Baptist roots. This way of reading Matthew 10 makes me want to go take a shower.

But providentially, a deeper dive reveals a different message entirely. In the beginning of the passage, Jesus says to his disciples, "A disciple is not above the teacher, nor a slave above the master. It is enough for the disciple to be like the teacher and the slave like the master." The word "disciple" in Greek simply means "learner." So to be a disciple of Jesus is to be a learner from Jesus. Discipleship means to ask this question: What is Jesus teaching, seeking to teach us, and what are we to learn from it? Perhaps the point of this passage is to pause and learn from Jesus who we are to be, what we are to say, and how we are to interact with others. Perhaps it's about what it means to be obedient to the Lord.

We tend to think of obedience in terms of power, and we think of power as control or domination. Someone has power, and someone else submits to that power and is thus obedient. We hear Jesus say, "I have not come to bring peace but a sword, and I have come to set a man against his father." If we read these verses with this understanding of obedience in mind, we end up right where we started, feeling like Jesus is calling us to be Christian militants. But notice what the sword in this passage actually is. It is not a weapon Jesus hands his disciples to take up. The very same saying appears in Luke's Gospel, and there the word is not "sword," but "division." The sword Jesus brings is the rupture that loyalty to him can drive through a household—the cost of discipleship, not its weapon.

The surrounding verses help us to see all of this in a different light. Jesus tells us that we are valued. We are called to have no fear of those who persecute us. Jesus tells us that secrets will become known, that things said in the dark should be told in the light. What is heard whispered should be proclaimed from the housetops. The disciples, and we, are not only called to learn from Jesus, but also to share the love we have received from him with those around us. While we Episcopalians aren't known for being enthusiastic evangelists, in fact, evangelism can be somewhat of a dirty word in our circles. The idea of being a fearless witness is not based on the authoritarian model of obedience in which one person submits to another because they have power over them and are afraid of them.

No, we are told not to fear each other, but to fear God, who gives Jesus the authority to proclaim these seemingly bizarre verses. Discipleship and the evangelism that necessarily comes with it is not something we do out of fear. It's not something we do out of obedience to someone who has power and to whom we are subservient. Discipleship and evangelism are things we do without fear, out of obedience to the one who took up his cross for our sake and gave everything to redeem us. The word "obedience" actually means to listen intently and to respond. To be obedient to Christ is to listen to him and to respond.

This virtue of Christian obedience is given an entire chapter in St. Benedict's monastic rule from the 6th century. In order to listen to the voice of Jesus, St. Benedict calls on his monks to listen to their abbot, to their other superiors, and to the voices of the other monks. You and I, of course, are not Benedictine monks, but the principle still applies. We are called to be obedient to Christ by listening both to the voices of those who have authority over us and to the voices of all those around us. That is to say, obedience is listening to the voice of God wherever it may be found and responding.

This may sound easy, but every time we face a choice or make a decision, we find ourselves in particular circumstances to which we must be obedient—whether it's at work, at home, with friends, or at church. There are obvious relationships where obedience is expected. Priests are expected to be obedient to their bishop. Workers are supposed to be obedient to their boss. Children to their parents, etc. But Christian obedience is to listen to the voice of Christ in all those around us and to respond. I'm called to listen to the voice of Christ in the voice of my spouse, in the voices of my friends, my nieces, and in the voices of all of you.

Sometimes we hear the voice of God and say to ourselves, "Fine, I guess I will change my behavior. It's not really what I want to do, but I'll do it because I'm supposed to." In his rules, St. Benedict doesn't call for reluctant obedience that manifests as mere outward conformity despite our grumblings, but rather an interior obedience that comes cheerfully, freely, and gladly. He says that unhesitating obedience comes naturally to those who cherish Christ above all.

Dear friends, unhesitating obedience to Jesus does indeed come with a cost. That division Jesus named, the sword that is not a weapon but a rupture, can run right through our closest relationships. Jesus said, "I have not come to bring peace but a sword. I have come to set a man against his father and a daughter against her mother." Sometimes obedience to Christ costs us dearly. It may cause division in our relationships, even within our own families. But thanks be to God, Jesus promises us that those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.

We hear a similar promise from St. Paul in our second lesson: "If we have been united with him in a death like his, we will certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his." I don't think that Jesus's words in this strange passage are designed to turn us all into militant Christians who love to sing "Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus." Rather, today's call is to be a disciple of Christ, to learn from him who we are to be, what we are to say, and how we are to interact with others. We are called to unhesitating, joyful obedience to Christ.
